passage: In the staff room of the government school, the new timetable was pinned up, and Jyoti's stomach dropped. Her Friday afternoon free period, her favourite, was gone. She had a refusal half written when Rehana, the vice-principal, pointed out that she had also gained a free period on Monday morning. Jyoti put down her pen. She tried a small experiment in her head: if someone offered her a Monday free period in exchange for her Friday one, just an even swap, would she take it? She pictured Monday mornings, the pile of weekend homework to check, the calm before the week. Honestly, yes. The Friday loss had only felt bigger because it was hers. She tore up the refusal.

qa.q: Which free period did Jyoti gain?
qa.a: Jyoti gained a free period on Monday morning.

qa.q: Why did Jyoti's stomach drop when she saw the timetable?
qa.a: Losing her favourite Friday free period felt like having something of hers taken away, which hit harder than a gain she hadn't noticed yet.

qa.q: What made Jyoti's small experiment useful?
qa.a: Imagining an even swap put the loss and the gain side by side at the same size, so she could see what she truly preferred instead of reacting to the loss.

qa.q: How might Rehana feel when Jyoti tears up the refusal?
qa.a: Rehana may feel relieved and appreciated, since pointing out the Monday gain helped settle a tricky timetable. 🙂

grounding: Shows a woman imagining a loss and a gain of equal size to check which she truly prefers, easing her pull toward keeping what she had.

passage:
Hi Mehak,
You asked if I'm taking the Bengaluru offer. I nearly said no straight away. All I could think about was what I'd lose: Sunday lunches with Mummy, who still calls me her baby girl, my running group, knowing every lane in Indore. Then I tried something my old manager taught me. I wrote each loss next to a gain just as big. Losing Sunday lunches versus gaining a team where I'd learn twice as fast. Losing my running group versus a new one there; there are plenty. Then I asked: if I already lived in Bengaluru, would I move back here for the same trade? Honestly, no. The losses only shouted louder because they're mine now. I'm saying yes. Visit me?
Disha

qa.q: Which offer is Disha considering?
qa.a: Disha is considering the Bengaluru offer.

qa.q: Why did Disha nearly say no straight away?
qa.a: Disha felt sad and reluctant because she could only think about what she'd lose, like Sunday lunches and her running group. Those are hers now, so they felt heavier than the gains.

qa.q: Which of Disha's steps helped most, and why?
qa.a: Asking whether she'd move back for the same trade if she already lived in Bengaluru helped most, because it flips the starting point and shows her true preference.

qa.q: How might Mummy feel about Disha's decision?
qa.a: Mummy may feel sad about missing Sunday lunches but proud that her daughter weighed it carefully and chose to grow.

grounding: Shows a young woman setting equal-sized losses and gains side by side and flipping her starting point to ease the tilt toward staying.

passage: Francis, you asked how I decided about the flat. I'm Ankita, the girl my mother says never moves. My landlord offered me a swap: same rent, but instead of my tiny old flat, a bigger one in his newer building across town. My first reaction was no way. I'd lose my balcony with the neem tree, the tea stall downstairs, my ten-minute walk to the bus. Then I did something that felt silly. I imagined I already lived in the new flat and someone offered me my old one in exchange. Would I take it? Losing a second bedroom, a quiet street, a kitchen with a window... I wouldn't. That told me my no was mostly about losing what was mine, not about which flat was better.

qa.q: What did the landlord offer Ankita?
qa.a: The landlord offered a swap: same rent, but a bigger flat in his newer building across town.

qa.q: Why was Ankita's first reaction "no way"?
qa.a: Ankita felt reluctant to lose things that were hers, like the neem-tree balcony and the tea stall. Those losses felt bigger than the new flat's gains.

qa.q: What made Ankita's imagined reverse swap useful?
qa.a: Picturing the offer the other way round put both flats on equal footing, so she could see that her no was about ownership, not about which flat was better.

qa.q: How might Francis react to the story?
qa.a: Francis may find the reverse-swap trick clever and worth trying for any big change where the familiar option feels safer.

grounding: Shows a young woman imagining the same trade from the other side to weigh loss and gain evenly before deciding.

passage: I'm Shalini, and I watched my cousin Lalremsiami make a decision in her little weaving room in Aizawl last month. A cooperative had offered to take her shawls: steady monthly orders, but they would set the prices. She'd always set her own. At first she said, "No way. I'll lose my freedom." That seemed to be the whole story for her. Then she did something I've never seen anyone do. She took a notebook and drew two columns. On one side she wrote what she'd lose: choosing prices, some special orders. On the other, what she'd gain: regular money, no chasing buyers. She tried to make them the same size. Then she asked herself aloud, "If I already had the steady orders, would I trade them for price freedom?" She thought for a long time. "No," she said. I don't know everything she felt, but she signed the next day.

qa.q: What did the cooperative offer Lalremsiami?
qa.a: Steady monthly orders, but they would set the prices.

qa.q: Why did Lalremsiami first say "No way"?
qa.a: Losing her freedom to set prices felt huge and immediate, so at first it drowned out the gain of steady orders.

qa.q: What question did Lalremsiami ask herself, and how did it help her decide?
qa.a: She asked, if she already had the steady orders, would she trade them for price freedom. Turning the gain into something she might lose made both sides weigh evenly, and she chose the orders.

qa.q: How might Shalini see Lalremsiami after watching this?
qa.a: Shalini seems impressed and curious, calling it something never seen before, and may try the two-column method too.

grounding: A cousin watches a young weaver weigh an equal loss and gain in two columns and ask which she would truly prefer, easing her pull toward the safe option.

passage:
Tuesday. Dilnaz got the offer: a job with a higher monthly salary but no year-end bonus. Her current job paid less each month but gave a bonus that made the total about the same. "I can't give up the bonus," she told her friend Zeenat at once. "What if the new place doesn't work out?"
Thursday. Zeenat came over with samosas. "Try this. Imagine you're already at the new job. Would you swap the higher monthly pay for a bonus that might come?" Dilnaz laughed. "When you say it like that, the bonus sounds risky." She took a sheet of paper and wrote both options in the same words: what she'd lose, what she'd gain, same size.
Saturday. She read the page again with fresh eyes. The totals really were about equal. What she actually wanted was the steadier monthly money for rent. She emailed the new company. "I accept."

qa.q: What did the new job not offer?
qa.a: No year-end bonus.

qa.q: Why did Dilnaz first say "I can't give up the bonus"?
qa.a: Losing something she already had felt much bigger than gaining an equal amount, so the safe option of staying felt right without her really comparing.

qa.q: What did Zeenat suggest, and why did it change Dilnaz's view?
qa.a: Zeenat asked her to imagine already having the new job and whether she'd swap it for the bonus. Flipping which side counted as the loss let Dilnaz weigh both evenly.

qa.q: How might Zeenat feel when Dilnaz accepts the new job?
qa.a: Zeenat is probably glad to have helped Dilnaz think clearly rather than pushing her either way.

grounding: A young woman imagines an equal loss and gain from both sides before deciding on a job, easing her automatic pull toward staying.

passage: Indu, you're scared to take the Bengaluru posting because of what you'd give up here. Let your old Vandana ma'am tell you what I did at twenty-five. The bank offered me a transfer to a new branch, a bigger role. All I could think about was losing: my flat near Amma, my evening walks with friends, my known desk. So one night I sat with a notebook and wrote two lines of the same size. "I lose my evening walks with friends." "I gain a team of my own to lead." Then I asked myself: if both were offered fresh, which would I truly want? Side by side, the loss didn't look so huge. I took the transfer. I missed the walks, honestly. But I never regretted it.

qa.q: What did the bank offer young Vandana?
qa.a: A transfer to a new branch, with a bigger role.

qa.q: What was young Vandana feeling before she wrote the two lines?

qa.q: What was the turning point in Vandana's story, and why did it help?
qa.a: Writing a loss and a gain of the same size side by side and asking which she would truly want; it shrank the automatic pull toward staying.

qa.q: How might Vandana's friends have felt about her leaving?
qa.a: They probably missed the evening walks too, and may have felt sad but proud of her new role.

grounding: A senior woman recalls writing an equal loss and gain side by side to decide on a transfer, easing her pull toward the safe option.

passage: The fellowship office wanted an answer by 9 p.m., and at seven the power went out across Lavanya's lane. By candlelight, her phone at eleven percent, she sat with Charu on the steps. "Every time I think of it, I just see what I'd lose," Lavanya said. "The permanent post. Everyone saying I threw it away." Charu handed her a notebook. "Then make them the same size. Write one real loss and one real gain." Lavanya wrote: "I give up two years in a permanent job." Then: "I gain two years of work I actually believe in." She looked at the two lines in the flickering light. "If someone offered me either one fresh, which would I pick?" The answer came quicker than she expected. At 8:47 she typed yes, with four percent battery left.

qa.q: How much battery was left when Lavanya typed yes?
qa.a: Four percent.

qa.q: What was Lavanya feeling before Charu handed her the notebook?
qa.a: She felt anxious and stuck, seeing only the losses: the permanent post and people saying she threw it away.

qa.q: What did the two-line exercise do for Lavanya?
qa.a: Writing a loss and a gain of the same size and asking which she would pick fresh eased the automatic pull toward the safe job.

qa.q: What is it like for Charu to sit with Lavanya in the power cut?
qa.a: Charu seems calm and caring, offering a simple tool rather than telling Lavanya what to choose.

grounding: Under a deadline and a power cut, a young woman writes an equal loss and gain side by side and asks which she would truly prefer.

passage: Afreen had been saying "maybe next month" about the Gomti Nagar flat for four months. Her office was there; her family home in the old city was an hour and a half away each side. On Sunday her sister Mehak found her circling the listing again. "What's stopping you?" "I'll lose Ammi's cooking. My room. The neighbourhood." Mehak took a pen. "Now the other side, same size." Afreen thought. "I gain three hours a day." She wrote both lines on the back of an electricity bill and stared. "If I lived in Gomti Nagar already, would I move somewhere that added three hours of travel just for my old room?" "Would you?" Afreen laughed. "No." She messaged the owner that evening, and promised Ammi every Sunday lunch.

qa.q: How long was Afreen's commute each way?
qa.a: An hour and a half each side.

qa.q: Why had Afreen kept saying maybe next month?
qa.a: She felt afraid of losing Ammi's cooking, her room and the neighbourhood, so staying felt safer even though the flat made sense.

qa.q: What question helped Afreen see the choice evenly?
qa.a: Whether, if she already lived near work, she would move somewhere that added three hours of travel just for her old room.

qa.q: How might Ammi feel about Afreen's promise?
qa.a: Ammi may feel sad to see her go but comforted by the promise of every Sunday lunch.

grounding: A young woman writes a loss and a gain of equal size and flips the question around, easing her pull toward staying put.

"Kiran, you've been staring at that offer letter for an hour."
"I know, Vishal. The new job pays more and it's more interesting. But I'd lose my team here. And the short commute."
"So you're saying no?"
"I think so. It's safer."
"Can I try something? Imagine two cases. In one, you lose the commute and the team. In the other, you gain the same amount: better work, more growth. If they were exactly the same size, which would you pick?"
Kiran thought for a long moment. "When you say it like that, the gain seems bigger. It's just that losing feels louder."
"Right."
"The commute's thirty minutes more. I could read on the train."
"And the team?"
"I'd miss them. But I'd make a new one."
She picked up a pen and wrote a list with two columns, weighing each side.

qa.q: How much longer would Kiran's new commute be?
qa.a: Thirty minutes more.

qa.q: Why did Kiran first lean toward saying no?
qa.a: Losing her team and short commute felt louder than the gains, so the safe option felt right, and she felt anxious about change.

qa.q: How did Vishal's exercise help Kiran?
qa.a: Imagining a loss and a gain of the same size let Kiran compare them evenly, easing the pull toward the safe choice.

qa.q: How does Vishal seem to help without deciding for Kiran?
qa.a: Vishal offers a simple way to think and asks questions, leaving the decision to Kiran.

grounding: It shows a thoughtful person who imagines a loss and gain of the same size and asks which she'd really prefer, easing the tilt toward safety.

passage: Last year I was offered a chance to move from the Delhi office to the new Pune branch as a team lead. My first reaction was no. I'd lose my flat, my Sunday badminton group, my mother's weekly visits. Every loss felt huge. My friend Amandeep suggested an odd exercise. "Write the loss, and then a gain the same size. Then ask which you'd really choose." So I wrote: lose badminton group, gain leading a team. Lose the flat, gain a new city. I sat with each pair, trying to feel them as equal. Some losses were still heavier; my mother's visits mattered more. But the badminton, the flat? The gains were bigger once I looked evenly. I took the job and arranged to fly home once a month. I still miss things. But I'm glad. Simran, a woman who nearly said no out of habit.

qa.q: What did Simran fear losing by moving to Pune?
qa.a: Her flat, her Sunday badminton group and her mother's weekly visits.

qa.q: How did Simran feel at first about the offer, and what changed?
qa.a: Simran felt that every loss was huge and wanted to say no, but after weighing each pair evenly, felt clearer and more confident.

qa.q: Why did pairing each loss with an equal gain help Simran decide?
qa.a: It reduced the automatic weight of losses, showing that some gains were bigger while some losses, like her mother's visits, still mattered.

qa.q: How might Amandeep feel seeing Simran take the job?
qa.a: Amandeep might feel pleased and a little proud that the exercise helped.

grounding: It shows a thoughtful woman who pairs each loss with a gain of the same size and chooses more evenly, easing the tilt toward the safe option.

passage:
Mentoring note, Tuesday

Ankita came to me unsure about switching from a stable government job to a research role at a university. She kept listing what she would lose: job security, a fixed routine, the respect her family gives the government post. The gains she mentioned only briefly: work she loves, growth, a chance to publish.

I suggested an exercise. For each loss, imagine a gain of exactly the same size, and ask honestly which she would choose. She did it slowly. "Losing the routine versus gaining work I love... the work, honestly." For security, she chose security. So it wasn't one-sided.

She left saying she'd ask the university about a contract with some security. She seemed calmer, less pulled by fear alone.

— Naveen

qa.q: What did Ankita list first when unsure about switching?
qa.a: What she would lose: job security, a fixed routine, and the respect her family gives the government post.

qa.q: How did Ankita seem to feel after the exercise?
qa.a: Ankita seemed calmer and less pulled by fear, able to see which gains she valued more and which losses truly mattered.

qa.q: Why was Naveen's exercise useful even though Ankita chose security for one pair?
qa.a: It helped her weigh each side evenly, so her choice reflected real preferences rather than automatic fear of loss.

qa.q: How might Ankita's family see her possible switch?
qa.a: Her family might feel worried about losing the respect and security of the government post.

grounding: It shows, through a mentor's note, a thoughtful woman who imagines losses and gains of the same size to weigh a job switch more evenly.

passage:
Tuesday night

The Pune offer came through today. Better role, same pay. I should be thrilled. Instead I feel sick.

I spent all evening listing what I'd lose: my flat, my Thursday dance class, being near Bidisha, knowing the city. The list got longer and longer.

Then I noticed I hadn't written a single thing I'd gain.

So I did an experiment. I imagined losing the dance class. How bad? Honestly, a 6. Then I imagined gaining a role where I'd lead a small team, which I've wanted for two years. How good? An 8.

I did it for each thing. Loss of the flat: 5. Gain of new people, new projects: 7.

When I put them side by side, Pune looked better. But my gut still wanted to stay. Losses just shout louder.

I'm going to sleep on it. But I feel calmer. I'm weighing things now, not just panicking.

Rashmi

qa.q: What did Rashmi score losing the dance class?
qa.a: Honestly, a 6.

qa.q: How did Rashmi feel before doing the experiment?
qa.a: Rashmi felt sick and anxious, focused only on the growing list of losses.

qa.q: What did Rashmi's experiment do well?
qa.a: Scoring each loss and gain of similar size side by side eased the automatic pull toward staying, so Rashmi could weigh the choice fairly.

qa.q: How might Bidisha feel if Rashmi moves to Pune?
qa.a: Bidisha might feel sad to lose having Rashmi nearby, but also happy for Rashmi's new role.

grounding: A thoughtful young adult imagines equal losses and gains for a job move and asks which is truly preferred, easing the tilt to safety.

passage:
In Neelam's village near Nashik, her family had grown onions on the same five acres for thirty years. At twenty-five, Neelam wanted to try grapes on one acre, like the neighbours had.

Her brother Lalit shook his head. "What if we lose the onion money from that acre?"

Neelam felt that fear too. It sat heavy in her stomach. But she did something her agriculture teacher had taught her. She sat on the verandah with a notebook and imagined both sides the same size.

If the grapes failed, they'd lose one acre's onion income for a year. If the grapes worked, they'd gain perhaps twice that, every year after.

"Lalit, imagine losing one acre's onions. Now imagine gaining double that. Which would you really choose, if both felt the same size?"

Lalit was quiet. "The gain. But the loss feels bigger."

"That's the tilt," she said. "Let's ask the agriculture officer about it next week, then decide."

qa.q: How many acres did Neelam's family farm?
qa.a: The same five acres for thirty years.

qa.q: What was Neelam feeling about trying grapes?
qa.a: Neelam felt the fear of losing the onion money heavy in her stomach, but also hopeful about the gain.

qa.q: What did Neelam do to weigh the choice fairly, and what is her next step?
qa.a: Neelam imagined the loss and gain at the same size to counter the tilt, and plans to ask the agriculture officer before deciding.

qa.q: How does Lalit see the choice after Neelam's question?
qa.a: Lalit admits he'd choose the gain, but the loss still feels bigger to him.

grounding: A young farmer imagines a loss and a gain of the same size and asks which she truly prefers, easing the pull toward the familiar crop.

passage: Emil found Chidi on the stairwell of their building in Utrecht, holding the landlord's letter. The top-floor flat was free: a balcony facing the canal, the same rent, but twenty minutes further from the hospital where she worked. "So? Swap?" Emil asked. "My gut says no," Chidi said. "I'd lose my short ride." She sat on the step and tried something. Suppose she already lived upstairs. Would she give up the balcony, the morning light, the herbs she kept meaning to grow, just to save twenty minutes of cycling along the water? She laughed. "No. I wouldn't trade it back." "Then your gut was just scared of moving," Emil said. Chidi folded the letter carefully. "Maybe. Let me sleep on it, with both sides written down in front of me."

qa.q: What did the top-floor flat offer?
qa.a: A balcony facing the canal at the same rent, but twenty minutes further from the hospital.

qa.q: Why did Chidi's first reaction lean towards saying no?
qa.a: Losing the short ride felt heavier than gaining the balcony, so staying put felt safe and comfortable before she had weighed both sides.

qa.q: Which trick helped Chidi, and why?
qa.a: She imagined already living upstairs and asked whether she would give up the balcony for a shorter ride; flipping the frame made the gain feel as real as the loss.

qa.q: How does Emil see Chidi's first reaction?
qa.a: Emil sees it as nerves about moving rather than a real preference, and gently nudges Chidi to look at both sides.

grounding: Shows a thoughtful person imagining a gain and a loss of the same size to check which she truly prefers, easing the pull toward staying put.
